datasource_item.source_question_text:
7. A Chinook salmon can jump out of water with a speed \(v_0\) and an angle \(\theta\) above the horizontal. What is the speed of the fish when it is at the maximum height?
A. \(v_0\).
B. \(v_0 \cos \theta\).
C. \(v_0 \sin \theta\).
D. 0.
datasource_item.generated_question_text:
Q7. A soccer ball is kicked with a speed $v_0$ at an angle $\theta$ above the horizontal. What is the speed of the ball when it is at the maximum height? (Neglect air resistance.)
A. $v_0$.
The speed is not generally the launch speed because the vertical component decreases to zero at the top.
B. $v_0\cos\theta$.
At maximum height the vertical velocity is zero while the horizontal component remains $v_0\cos\theta$, so the speed equals $v_0\cos\theta$.
C. $v_0\sin\theta$.
This is the initial vertical component, but at maximum height the vertical component is zero.
D. 0.
Only the vertical component becomes zero at the top; the horizontal component generally remains nonzero.

The probe’s mass does not appear in $v=\sqrt{2GM/R}$, so escape speed is independent of the escaping object’s mass.

This repeats the misconception that escape speed depends on the object’s mass, which it does not in this formula.

Because $v \propto \sqrt{M/R}$, decreasing $M$ and increasing $R$ both make $v$ smaller, not larger.

Since $v \propto \sqrt{M/R}$, increasing $M$ and decreasing $R$ both increase the escape speed.
